title: AMAZING NEWS: DEA KICKS CAN DOWN ROAD Regarding Telemedicine Prescribing of Controlled Substances.
subtitle: This newsletter is taking all the credit.
text:
I did it.

I complained in a newsletter and single-handedly—along with the other 38,369 public commenters that I am ignoring as a matter of farcical best practice—got the following extension of controlled substance prescribing by telehealth! I absolutely predicted this…cause I’m super special and important. I’ve been an honorable-mention change maker since 2016. Much like the DEA, I’ve been almost getting it right for years now. In the case of this telemedicine thing, there may have been some larger public health issues.

In other words, if a patient and a practitioner have established a telemedicine relationship on or before November 11, 2023, the same telemedicine flexibilities that have governed the relationship to that point are permitted until November 11, 2024.

Nothing says success like this extension of uncertainty into the near future!

DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH AND HUMAN SERVICES
42 CFR Part 12
Temporary Extension of COVID-19 Telemedicine Flexibilities for Prescription of Controlled Medications
AGENCY: Drug Enforcement Administration, Department of Justice; Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, Department of Health and Human Services.

That's right, we did it, or I did it all by myself. Cerebral prescribed too many stimulants. I get it. But now…There is a temporary rule!

The story, as told by the DEA, downplays this newsletter’s role, but they kind of can't look cool if they admit how influential I am:

On March 1, 2023 the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), in concert with the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), promulgated two notices of proposed rulemakings (NPRMs) soliciting comments on proposals to allow for prescribing of controlled medications pursuant to the practice of telemedicine in instances where the prescribing practitioner has never conducted an in-person medical evaluation of the patient.

….along with the minor detail of 38,369 additional public comments— were, in getting a can kicked down the road:

DATES: This rule is effective May 11, 2023, through November 11, 2024.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: Scott A. Brinks, Diversion Control Division, Drug Enforcement Administration; Mailing Address: 8701 Morrissette Drive, Springfield, VA 22152, Telephone: (571) 776-3882.

My advocacy, along with a few other concerned citizens and some news here and there, led to this sequence of events:

On March 1, 2023, DEA, in concert with HHS, promulgated two NPRMs in the Federal Register – “Telemedicine prescribing of controlled substances when the practitioner and the patient have not had a prior in-person medical evaluation”3 (the General Telemedicine Rule) and “Expansion of induction of buprenorphine via telemedicine encounter”4 (the Buprenorphine Rule) – which proposed to expand patient access to prescriptions for controlled medications via telemedicine encounters relative to the pre-COVID-19 PHE landscape. The purpose of the two proposed rules was to make permanent some of the telemedicine flexibilities established during the COVID-19 PHE in order to facilitate patient access to controlled medications via telemedicine when consistent with public health and safety, while maintaining effective controls against diversion. The comment period for these two NPRMs closed on March 31, 2023. Those NPRMs generated a total of 38,369 public comments – 35,454 comments on the General Telemedicine Rule and 2,915 comments on the Buprenorphine Rule.

And because what we've all been waiting for is additional uncertainty, I am thrilled to announce that we got it. I won. We all won-ish.

The canned has been kicked down the road in a way that continues to provide endless uncertainty for prescribers of controlled substances managing patients in their job as medical professionals:

After reviewing those comments, DEA, jointly with SAMHSA, is issuing this temporary rule to effectuate the following:

The full set of telemedicine flexibilities regarding the prescription of controlled medications as were in place during the COVID-19 PHE will remain in place through November 11, 2023.

Additionally, for any practitioner-patient telemedicine relationships that have been or will be established on or before November 11, 2023, the full set of telemedicine flexibilities regarding prescription of controlled medications as were in place during the COVID-19 PHE will continue to be permitted via a one-year grace period through November 11, 2024. In other words, if a patient and a practitioner have established a telemedicine relationship on or before November 11, 2023, the same telemedicine flexibilities that have governed the relationship to that point are permitted until November 11, 2024.

It’s important to note that “telemedicine flexibilities” apply as long as a patient realizes they need help before November 2023:

This temporary rule also extends the COVID-19 PHE telemedicine flexibilities through November 11, 2024, as applied to any practitioner-patient relationships established via telemedicine encounters on or before November 11, 2023. In other words, as long as a practitioner and patient have established a telemedicine relationship on or before November 11, 2023, the pandemic telemedicine flexibilities will be extended through November 11, 2024, as to that established relationship.

OK, I'm going to stop the silliness now.

Welcome to My Keynote

I want to make this very clear to everyone working in our regulatory agencies: those of us who want to comply with all appropriate rules and regulations are important. But the most important people are our patients.

What patients need is medical care. They don't need telemedical care. They need medical care when they have a medical condition that requires it.

It is 2023. The Internet exists. Zoom exists. Phones exist. These things have existed for a very long time. We have endless technologies that would allow us to appropriately limit diversion and enhance our ability to comply with all appropriate rules and regulations.

We don't need endless uncertainty about who can get the care and in what ways dictated by regulatory agencies that happen to control some of the drugs we need to treat some of our patients.

I understand the diversion is a problem. The bigger problem is that people doing diversion of controlled substances are generally drug dealers. They are very interested in using breaking the law to make a lot of money without having to comply with your regulations. I do not hate drug dealers, and I do not hate the DEA. People will access drugs they want to put in their brains. Or bodies. Some of those drugs will be to manage medical conditions and prescribed by medical professionals.

But we have to recognize that diversion, a.k.a. regulatory arbitrage by people with higher risk tolerance and lower access to the kinds of socioeconomic status that physicians with DEA licenses have, needs to be considered as part of the equation. Selling drugs illegally is illegal, and the people doing that can and should be prosecuted to the full extent of the law… until we decriminalize those things as well.

The war on drugs is a catastrophic failure. The attempt to create endless barriers to the appropriate prescribing of controlled substances has led to this utterly bizarre world where pharmaceutical companies are leveraging medical doctors to get people addicted to things they shouldn't be on. The reaction to that has been for the DEA to crack down and create a massive incentive for illegally distributed drugs like fentanyl and xylazine to lead to the death of hundreds of thousands.

We created this problem ourselves. So when you revise the rules and regulations, let's make it easy to comply. Let's make medical care something that is as easier than it needs to be.

And that way—-instead of getting diverted controlled substances from street drug dealers doing things that make sense in their cultural context—we can make getting medical care easy and accessible.

No one abusing fentanyl all day is doing so because they're having a great day. They're not doing so because they have no problems. They probably have problems that could be addressed with appropriate medical care. Instead, we put barriers to care in their way. Then they use fentanyl on the street and die.

I'm sick of it. You should be sick of it. Let's make regulations that work, and that enhance everyone's ability to comply with all appropriate rules and regulations. Let's make medical care something patients can get when they need it. Let's pay for treatments that are wildly effective and safe. Let's make access to care—appropriately regulated—the cornerstone of our approach. Let's make sure that diversion isn't what people have to turn to because they can't get a goddamn medical appointment, and they go broke if they try to get one.

I'm sorry, it looks like I've dropped my mic. That's gonna be a compliance issue. I'm gonna go look for it. This is not a meaningful mission accomplished. We need to work together with regulators to make sure patient get the care they need, but for the moment, this will have to do.

—Owen Scott Muir, M.D.
